title: The Bus, the Bird and the Courtroom: from El Valle to Sunset Park
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: El Valle, the Wheel, and the Gate at Yare

stops.name: El Valle, Caracas: the birth in the parish
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; CIDOB political biography). Day and year firm. The pin is the parish of El Valle, not a hospital or a street: no source reviewed documents either. Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal later affirmed Caracas as the birthplace against an opposition claim of Cúcuta, Colombia.
stops.campa: A son is born in the parish of El Valle, on the southern edge of Caracas, to Nicolás Maduro García, a union man of the Venezuelan left, and Teresa de Jesús Moros. The house is a working-class house and the politics in it are inherited rather than chosen: union business gets done at the kitchen table, and the boy hears the vocabulary of organized labour long before he has any use for it. No hospital and no street survive in the record, only the parish. Opponents will later put the birth across the border in Cúcuta, Colombia. The Supreme Tribunal rules on that claim and affirms Caracas.
suggested_refs: The parish of El Valle, southern Caracas, and its 1960s union households
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
CIDOB political biography (cidob.org)

stops.name: Liceo José Ávalos: the diploma that is not there
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Sources give only the 1970s and early 1980s for his schooling; the date here orders the segment and is not attested to the year. The pin is approximate to the El Valle parish, the school building not independently located. Record-based reporting says he did not complete the requirements for the secondary diploma; other biographies call him a graduate. The contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: He attends the public liceo on the same streets he was born on, and takes to student politics before he takes to anything else. Reporting based on school records says he leaves without completing the requirements for the secondary diploma; several biographies call him a graduate anyway, and the two accounts have never been reconciled in public. No source reviewed names a subject he studied or a year he left, and which version is right is not settled by anything now in the record. He does not attend a university, then or later.
suggested_refs: The public Liceo José Ávalos, El Valle, and its student politics of the late 1970s
sources: Deep-research dossier synthesis of biographical reporting on school records
Britannica and EBSCO Research Starters profiles, both noting no university degree

stops.name: Caracas: joining the Liga Socialista
stops.date_confidence: attested for the affiliation, reconstruction for the year and the formal status. es.wikipedia gives c. 1977 and later seats on the Comité Nacional and the Comité Regional de Caracas; other journalistic profiles push the affiliation into the 1980s. The corrected earlier date is used here and the disagreement is flagged rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Around 1977 he joins the Liga Socialista, a party grown out of the wreck of the Venezuelan guerrilla of the sixties, and in time sits on both its national committee and its Caracas regional committee. Chavismo does not exist. Hugo Chávez is an unknown lieutenant in the army. What exists is a small, disciplined left that reads Marx, argues about the road, and works the unions. The formal shape of his membership varies from source to source, and so does the year he joined. The work it puts him to is the ordinary work of a cadre party: meetings, and the patient count of who can be relied on.
suggested_refs: The Liga Socialista and the post-guerrilla Venezuelan left of the 1970s
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Nicolás Maduro'
Multiple journalistic profiles (chronology and formal status vary)

stops.name: Havana: the year in the cadre school
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The fact of a year of Cuban political training around 1986 is well attested; the school is genuinely disputed. en.wikipedia names the Young Communists' Escuela Nacional de Cuadros Julio Antonio Mella; es.wikipedia and Runrun.es name the Communist Party's Ñico López school. Both cannot be right. The coordinates are roughly correct only for the Ñico López reading, in the Plaza de la Revolución municipality. Month and day are an ordering device.
stops.campa: A scholarship from the Liga Socialista sends him to Havana for roughly a year of political formation: Marxist philosophy, political economy, the strategy of revolution taught as a trade. He is twenty-three, and this year of cadre school is the whole of his education past the liceo. The sources do not agree on which school took him. Some name the Julio Antonio Mella cadre school of the Young Communists, others the Ñico López school of Fidel Castro's party. The curriculum is undocumented and the dates are loose. Which of the two buildings held him for that year is a question the record has not answered.
suggested_refs: The two candidate Havana cadre schools: Escuela Nacional de Cuadros Julio Antonio Mella (UJC) and Escuela Superior del Partido Ñico López (PCC)
sources: Runrun.es, 'Maduro se formó en Cuba desde 1986'
en.wikipedia, 'Nicolás Maduro'
es.wikipedia, 'Nicolás Maduro'

stops.name: Caracas Metro: the wheel and the union
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact, reconstruction for the year. Britannica and multiple pre-presidency profiles place the bus driving in the late 1980s and the SITRAMECA leadership in the early 1990s. No depot or union office is documented in the sources reviewed; the pin is the Caracas Metro system generally.
stops.campa: He drives a bus in the Caracas public transport system and organizes the men who drive beside him, rising through SITRAMECA, the union of the metro workers. It is his first base that he does not inherit from his father: a payroll, a depot, a grievance, a strike vote. Here he learns the trade unionist's arithmetic of numbers and patience, which is the only training in government he will ever receive. No source reviewed names the depot he drove out of, or the office where SITRAMECA kept its books.
suggested_refs: SITRAMECA, the Caracas Metro workers' union, and the Metrobús depots of the early 1990s
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
InSight Crime and other pre-presidency journalistic profiles

stops.name: Caracas: the fourth of February and the prisoners' committees
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; standard historical record of the 1992 coup attempt). The date is the coup itself; Maduro's involvement in the release campaigns is dated by Britannica to 1992 without a finer division.
stops.campa: On the fourth of February a lieutenant colonel named Hugo Chávez leads a coup against Carlos Andrés Pérez, fails inside a day, and asks for a microphone to tell his men to lay down their arms. He goes to prison and comes out of the broadcast famous. Maduro, twenty-nine, throws himself into the committees campaigning for the prisoners' release, carrying petitions and turning out crowds for a man he has never met and will not meet for another two years.
suggested_refs: The 4 February 1992 coup attempt and the civilian committees for the release of its officers
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
Standard historical record of the Chávez biography

stops.name: Yare: the visit, and the gate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, with documentary support. The date of the first meeting is Maduro's own later public account, repeated in profiles and in Asamblea Nacional commemorative material; it is self-reported and not independently documented, and the geography and chronology lenses of the research pool tag it differently. Chávez's release date is itself contested: 26 March 1994 in Asamblea Nacional and RNV coverage, 27 March 1994 in es.wikipedia. Coordinates corrected to the prison site per Wikidata Q1498168.
stops.campa: He drives out to the prison at San Francisco de Yare, in the hills of Miranda, and there, by his own account, meets Chávez face to face for the first time, three days short of two years after the coup. The account is his; no independent record of the day has surfaced. In March 1994 the charges are dropped and Chávez walks out of that gate into a movement already waiting for him in the street. Maduro is by then inside it. So is a lawyer on the team that argued the prisoners out, Cilia Flores.
suggested_refs: The Cárcel de Yare, San Francisco de Yare, Simón Bolívar municipality, Miranda
sources: Maduro's own later public account, reported in multiple biographical profiles
CIDOB biography and Asamblea Nacional commemorative material
Wikidata Q1498168 for the prison coordinates

stops.name: Caracas: the MBR-200 builds an electoral vehicle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Britannica; EBSCO Research Starters). Month and day default to 01; no finer date for Maduro's role in the founding of the Movimiento Quinta República is given in the sources reviewed.
stops.campa: Inside the Movimiento Bolivariano Revolucionario 200, the network Chávez built among officers, the argument of the decade is settled: they will contest an election rather than attempt another barracks. The Movimiento Quinta República is built as the vehicle. Maduro works the civilian half of it: the unions, the neighbourhood committees, the transport workers. He is among the very few people from outside the army whom Chávez trusts with details, and no officer in the network knows how to run that half of it anyway.
suggested_refs: The MBR-200 and the founding papers of the Movimiento Quinta República
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
EBSCO Research Starters profile

stops.name: Palacio Federal Legislativo, Caracas: elected deputy
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; CIDOB). The November legislative elections; Chávez's presidential victory follows in December 1998.
stops.campa: In the legislative elections of November he wins a seat in the old Chamber of Deputies, his first national office, thirty-five years old and a decade out of the driver's seat of a bus. A month later Chávez takes the presidency outright and the whole apparatus of the Fourth Republic goes onto the table. The bicameral congress Maduro has just entered is already condemned by the programme he was elected on. He takes the seat on the eighth of November 1998 and holds it for a year.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Federal Legislativo and the last Chamber of Deputies of the Venezuelan Fourth Republic
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
CIDOB political biography

stops.name: Palacio Federal Legislativo, Caracas: the Constituent Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Britannica; EBSCO; CIDOB). Month and day are an ordering device set near the installation of the assembly; the sources reviewed give only 1999 for Maduro's membership.
stops.campa: He is elected to the National Constituent Assembly, which spends the year writing a new constitution and writing into it a new name for the country: the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, after Simón Bolívar, dead a hundred and sixty-nine years and now the official ancestor of the state. The assembly dissolves the congress Maduro was elected to and replaces it with a single chamber, ending his own first mandate. He votes for it. The sources reviewed give only the year of his membership, not the month he took his seat.
suggested_refs: The 1999 Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
EBSCO Research Starters
CIDOB political biography

stops.name: Palacio Federal Legislativo, Caracas: president of the Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Britannica; CIDOB gives January 2005). He had sat as a deputy in the new unicameral National Assembly since the elections of 2000. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He is elected to the new unicameral National Assembly in 2000, spends five years in it, and in January 2005 is chosen its president, in a chamber the opposition has walked out of by boycott. The post puts him among the half-dozen senior figures of Chavismo and marks him as personally trusted by Chávez, in a movement where personal trust is the only currency that clears. He has no military rank and no degree. He holds the presidency of the Assembly until Chávez moves him to the foreign ministry in August 2006.
suggested_refs: The unicameral National Assembly created by the 1999 Constitution
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
CIDOB political biography

stops.name: Casa Amarilla, Caracas: six years as foreign minister
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Britannica; CIDOB). Day defaults to 01. The tenure of more than six years, to 2012, is attested across diplomatic profiles.
stops.campa: Chávez names him foreign minister in August 2006. From the Casa Amarilla, on the Plaza Bolívar, he runs the Cuban relationship, the oil diplomacy of the region, and the building of blocs designed to leave Washington out of the room. Diplomats who deal with him report a negotiator rather than an ideologue, which sets him apart from the rivals around him. Ministers in this government are moved like furniture. He keeps this one for more than six years, and leaves it only for the vice presidency.
suggested_refs: The Casa Amarilla, seat of the Venezuelan foreign ministry on the Plaza Bolívar
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
CIDOB political biography
Multiple diplomatic profiles

stops.name: Havana: the seat of government, kept in repair
stops.date_confidence: attested for the pattern of repeated official visits during the 2006-2012 tenure; the specific date is an ordering device and no individual visit is itemized in the sources reviewed. Coordinates corrected to the Palacio de la Revolución on the Plaza de la Revolución (en.wikipedia); the pin is the government quarter, not a documented meeting room.
stops.campa: The foreign minister comes to Havana again and again, to the seat of the Cuban government, to keep in repair the alliance that is the axis of Venezuelan foreign policy: doctors, teachers and intelligence officers moving one way, subsidized oil moving the other. The relationship survives Chávez, and survives the collapse of the oil price that paid for it. No single visit is itemized anywhere in the record; the pin is the government quarter of the city, not a room in it.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de la Revolución, Plaza de la Revolución, Havana
sources: Deep-research dossier synthesis of Maduro-era foreign-policy reporting
en.wikipedia, 'Plaza de la Revolución' for the corrected coordinates

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: made vice president
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Britannica; CIDOB; contemporary coverage of the October 2012 election). Day defaults to 01; the appointment follows the election of 7 October within days.
stops.campa: Chávez beats Henrique Capriles in the election of the seventh of October and within days makes Maduro executive vice president, an office in Venezuela that is given rather than won, lifting him over Diosdado Cabello and every other claimant inside the movement. In a government of soldiers a bus driver is now second in the state, and the succession has been settled without the word being used. The cancer that has been treated in Havana for a year and a half has not been beaten, and everyone in the palace knows it.
suggested_refs: The Palacio de Miraflores, seat of the Venezuelan presidency
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
CIDOB political biography
Contemporary press coverage of the October 2012 Venezuelan election

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the broadcast of the eighth of December
stops.date_confidence: attested (Venezuelan state broadcast of 8 December 2012, widely reported; transcript reproduced in Javier Biardeau R., 'El mensaje de Chávez el 8-12-2012'). The quote is taken from that transcript.
stops.campa: On the eve of leaving for another surgery in Havana, Chávez appears on national television with his cabinet ranged around him and does the thing no caudillo does: he names his successor out loud, in advance, on the record. It is the last time he speaks to Venezuela from Venezuelan soil. Maduro sits beside him and says nothing that anyone afterwards remembers. His opinion, Chávez tells the country, is firm, full as the full moon, irrevocable, absolute, total: elect Nicolás Maduro.
stops.quote: mi opinión firme, plena como la luna llena, irrevocable, absoluta, total, es que en ese escenario que obligaría a convocar como manda la Constitución de nuevo a elecciones presidenciales, ustedes elijan a Nicolás Maduro como presidente de la República Bolivariana de Venezuela
stops.quote_source: Hugo Chávez, cadena nacional, 8 December 2012, transcript reproduced in Javier Biardeau R., 'El mensaje de Chávez el 8-12-2012', rebelion.org, pp. 3-4
suggested_refs: The recording of the cadena nacional of 8 December 2012
sources: Contemporary Venezuelan state broadcast, widely reported (BBC, Reuters)
Biardeau transcript PDF, rebelion.org

stops.name: CIMEQ, Havana: the last surgery
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact and the place; the day is an ordering device. The research pool gives only December 2012 to March 2013 for the stay. Coordinates corrected to the Centro de Investigaciones Médico Quirúrgicas, Calle 216, Reparto Siboney, Playa, Havana.
stops.campa: Chávez is operated on at the Centro de Investigaciones Médico Quirúrgicas in the Siboney district of western Havana, another cancer surgery in a run of them. He is never seen in public in Venezuela again. Maduro travels to be there and, for three months, governs Venezuela by bulletin from a foreign hospital, reading out communiqués that grow shorter and less specific as the winter goes on, and that go on saying week after week that the president is recovering.
suggested_refs: The CIMEQ hospital, Reparto Siboney, Playa, Havana
sources: Deep-research dossier synthesis
CIMEQ address and location cross-checked against the Siboney listing

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the death announced
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; worldwide press coverage of 5 March 2013). The constitutional dispute over whether the vice president or the president of the National Assembly should have assumed the interim is a matter of record and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Maduro comes onto television flanked by the high command and tells the country that Hugo Chávez has died, at the Hospital Militar Dr. Carlos Arvelo in Caracas. He assumes executive authority the same day, as vice president. The opposition argues that the constitution hands the interim to the president of the National Assembly instead, and loses that argument in the Supreme Tribunal. Two decades after he carried petitions for the prisoner of Yare, the state Chávez built is his. The queues to see the body run through the city for days.
suggested_refs: The Hospital Militar Dr. Carlos Arvelo, Caracas, where Chávez died
sources: Britannica, 'Nicolas Maduro'
Widespread international press coverage, March 2013

stops.name: Academia Militar, Caracas: the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested (El Espectador, 'Chávez vive, la lucha sigue, grita Maduro en funeral de Chávez', March 2013). Cristina Fernández de Kirchner's arrival in Caracas on 5 March and her vigil at the military hospital chapel are attested in her own file's sources.
stops.campa: The coffin lies at the Military Academy in Caracas and the presidents of the region come to it. Cristina Fernández de Kirchner has been in the city since the day of the death, when she flew up from Buenos Aires and kept vigil in the chapel of the military hospital. Maduro gives the eulogy. He does not attempt Chávez's register, which nobody in the movement can attempt. He closes on the slogan the crowd already knows and shouts back at him: Chávez vive, la lucha sigue.
stops.quote: La batalla continúa, ¡Chávez vive, la lucha sigue! Que viva Hugo Chávez, que viva nuestro pueblo.
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, eulogy at Chávez's funeral, quoted in El Espectador, March 2013
suggested_refs: The Academia Militar de Caracas, where Chávez lay in state
sources: El Espectador, March 2013
cristina_fernandez_de_kirchner.journey.json, stop 'Caracas: the vigil for Chávez'

stops.name: Cuartel de la Montaña, Caracas: the body carried up
stops.date_confidence: attested. The mausoleum in the Monte Piedad sector of the 23 de Enero parish was inaugurated and the body moved there on 15 March 2013 (es.wikipedia); an earlier draft of the research pool gave July 2013, which is an error and is corrected here. Coordinates likewise corrected to the fort itself.
stops.campa: Ten days after the death the coffin is carried up into the 23 de Enero, to the Cuartel de la Montaña, the barracks Chávez himself attacked on the fourth of February 1992, converted now into a mausoleum with an honour guard. Maduro walks behind it through a barrio that has voted for Chavismo in every election it has been offered. He will come back up this hill on the anniversaries, in every year of his presidency, and a camera will be there each time. The date is the fifteenth of March, 2013.
suggested_refs: The Cuartel de la Montaña 4F, Monte Piedad, 23 de Enero, Caracas
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Cuartel de la Montaña'
CIDOB political biography
RNV coverage of the 2024 Yare-anniversary visit

stops.name: Sabaneta, Barinas: the pajarito
stops.date_confidence: attested for the episode and the words (EFE wire, 2 April 2013, reproduced in La Nación, Ecuavisa and Confirmado). The place is contested inside the research pool: the quote lens puts the remarks in Sabaneta, Barinas, on 2 April; the geography lens describes an elaboration at a rally in Catia La Mar, Vargas, on 9 April. Both may be true of a story he told repeatedly. The wording 'acá arriba', not 'aquí arriba', is the corrected reading.
stops.campa: Campaigning in Chávez's own state of Barinas, in the town where Chávez was born, Maduro tells the crowd what happened to him in a small chapel: a bird came in, very small, and circled three times over his head. It whistled at him a while, and he felt the spirit of his chief in it, and it blessed the campaign and left. He reports it as a thing that occurred. The opposition makes a year of jokes out of it and Leopoldo López suggests a psychiatric examination. The campaign puts the bird on the posters.
stops.quote: De repente entró un pajarito, chiquitico, y me dio tres vueltas acá arriba.
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, campaign remarks, EFE wire of 2 April 2013, as reproduced in La Nación (Argentina), 'Maduro dice que Chávez se le apareció en forma de pajarito chiquitico y lo bendijo'
suggested_refs: The chapel in Barinas of Maduro's account; the campaign posters carrying the bird
sources: La Nación (Argentina), 2 April 2013, reproducing the EFE wire
Ecuavisa and Confirmado.com.ve, same wire
Infobae, 'Maduro se pasea con el pajarito Chávez', 10 April 2013
Mercopress and HuffPost coverage of the April 2013 campaign

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the narrow election and the sash
stops.date_confidence: attested. The vote was held 14 April 2013 and the inauguration 19 April (CNN, ABC News, Washington Post). Final CNE figures are Maduro 7,587,579 (50.61 percent) to Capriles 7,363,980 (49.12 percent), a margin of 223,599 votes on turnout of 79.65 percent; an earlier draft of the research pool carried the election-night preliminary bulletin instead, and it is corrected here.
stops.campa: He wins the special election of the fourteenth by 223,599 votes out of nearly fifteen million cast, 50.61 percent against 49.12 for Henrique Capriles, and is sworn in five days later. Turnout is 79.65 percent. Capriles demands a full audit of the paper trail and does not get one that satisfies him. Chávez used to win by ten points and by twenty; this margin is 1.49. Whether the count of April 2013 was clean is a question nobody has since been able to close.
suggested_refs: The CNE final bulletin of the 14 April 2013 presidential election
sources: CNE results as reported by BBC and contemporary outlets
en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia, '2013 Venezuelan presidential election'
CNN, ABC News, Washington Post coverage of the inauguration

stops.name: Caracas: the eyes on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (Univision/N+; Wikipedia, 'Chávez eyes'). Month and day are an ordering device: the sources date the mandated display to 2013 without a finer division.
stops.campa: The stylized outline of Chávez's eyes, drawn for the 2012 campaign, is ordered onto billboards, ministry façades and the blocks of the Gran Misión Vivienda housing programme. It becomes the dominant state image of the Maduro years, painted on far more walls than any face of the living president. Municipal officials describe the intention without embarrassment: the gaze is to be perennial and eternal, watching over the city, accompanying the government wherever it goes.
suggested_refs: The ojos de Chávez graphic on the Gran Misión Vivienda blocks and ministry façades
sources: Univision/N+, 'A casi cuatro años de la muerte de Chávez, la imagen de sus ojos'
Wikipedia, 'Chávez eyes'

stops.name: Caracas: the marriage to Cilia Flores
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by multiple biographical profiles, which do not agree on the day and which the research pool flags for corroboration. Day defaults to 01. The partnership itself long predates the marriage.
stops.campa: He marries Cilia Flores, lawyer and deputy, for two decades already his partner inside the movement and, before that, one of the lawyers who argued the 1992 prisoners out of Yare. The Chavista press calls her the first combatant. She has been a deputy, president of the National Assembly and attorney general of the republic, and she will be a co-defendant on his indictment. The ceremony is not a public event, and the profiles that report it do not agree on the day.
suggested_refs: Cilia Flores, deputy, National Assembly president and attorney general before the marriage
sources: Multiple biographical profiles (deep-research dossier synthesis, flagged for corroboration)

stops.name: Palacio Federal Legislativo, Caracas: asking for the decree
stops.date_confidence: attested for the speech and its publication (Fondo Editorial de la Asamblea Nacional Willian Lara, published transcript, 2013; WorldCat record). Tagged as reconstruction in the research pool because the framing survives chiefly through the government's own printed edition.
stops.campa: He comes to the National Assembly in person to ask for the power to legislate by decree, framing the request as a war on corruption and on what he calls economic sabotage: the hoarding, the parallel dollar, the shelves that empty in an afternoon. The Assembly's own press prints the speech afterwards under the title ¡Voy a fondo, vamos con todo! The powers are granted. The parallel dollar, which is the real government of prices in Venezuela, goes on climbing through the year. The shelves do not fill.
suggested_refs: ¡Voy a fondo, vamos con todo! (Fondo Editorial de la Asamblea Nacional Willian Lara, 2013)
sources: Fondo Editorial de la Asamblea Nacional Willian Lara, published transcript, 2013
WorldCat catalogue record

stops.name: Caracas: the barricades of 2014
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year (widely documented international press coverage of the 2014 Venezuelan protests). February is the standard start of the protest wave; the research pool gives only 2014, so the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Students go into the streets over crime, scarcity and the price of everything, and stay there for months. The barricades acquire a name, guarimbas, and the dead are counted on both sides of them. Maduro governs against the street with the National Guard and against the shortage with price inspectors. Neither instrument does what it is supposed to do, and the queue outside the supermarket becomes an ordinary part of the day. Leopoldo López walks into custody in front of the cameras and is imprisoned.
suggested_refs: The 2014 Venezuelan protests and the imprisonment of Leopoldo López
sources: Widely documented international press coverage of the 2014 Venezuelan protests

stops.name: United Nations Headquarters, New York: the sixty-ninth General Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Comunicación e Información, printed edition of the speech, 2014). Day defaults to 01; the general debate of the sixty-ninth session opened on 24 September 2014.
stops.campa: He flies to New York and addresses the sixty-ninth General Assembly on sovereignty, empire, and a world with more than one centre in it. The general debate of the session opens on the twenty-fourth of September 2014. The information ministry prints the speech as a pamphlet for distribution at home, which is the audience that matters to it. It is his one appearance in the city as a head of state at liberty, and the only time he enters the United States of his own will.
suggested_refs: Intervención del presidente Nicolás Maduro en la 69° Asamblea General de la ONU (MINCI, 2014)
sources: Government pamphlet, Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Comunicación e Información, 2014

stops.name: Ciudad Belén, Miranda: the warning on television
stops.date_confidence: attested for the words and the date (ABC Internacional, 'Maduro amenaza con masacre y muerte si fracasa la revolución chavista', 6 June 2015, reporting a Venezolana de Televisión broadcast from Ciudad Belén, Miranda). An earlier draft of the research pool misattributed the remarks to El Mundo and to 1 July 2015 in Caracas; both are corrected here. The pin is approximate to the Guarenas area of Miranda, the housing development not independently located.
stops.campa: On state television, from a housing development in Miranda, he tells the country what failure would look like. Get ready, he says, for the massacre of the twenty-seventh of February to come back, and you will know it live, not from a video; get ready for a time of massacre and of death if the Bolivarian revolution fails. He is invoking the Caracazo of 1989, when the army fired into the poor barrios of Caracas. Six months later his party loses the legislative election. The broadcast goes out on Venezolana de Televisión on the sixth of June, 2015.
stops.quote: prepárense para un tiempo de masacre y de muerte si fracasa la revolución bolivariana
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, Venezolana de Televisión broadcast from Ciudad Belén, Miranda, 6 June 2015, quoted in ABC Internacional, 6 June 2015
suggested_refs: The Caracazo of 27 February 1989, invoked in the broadcast
sources: ABC (abc.es) Internacional, 6 June 2015

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the night of the 112 seats
stops.date_confidence: attested (PBS NewsHour coverage of the December 2015 Venezuelan legislative election).
stops.campa: On the sixth of December the opposition coalition takes 112 of 167 seats, a two-thirds supermajority, and Maduro goes on television the same night and acknowledges the result. It is the only national vote he loses and concedes, and he never withdraws the concession. Within weeks the outgoing Assembly packs the Supreme Tribunal, the Tribunal begins striking down the new Assembly's acts one by one, and inside a year the chamber the voters elected is a formality with no power to legislate.
suggested_refs: The December 2015 National Assembly election and the opposition supermajority
sources: PBS NewsHour coverage of the December 2015 Venezuelan legislative election

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the name on the Treasury list
stops.date_confidence: attested (U.S. Department of the Treasury designation announcement, 31 July 2017). The designation was made in Washington; the stop sits at Maduro's own seat of government, where he received it, rather than at the Treasury building he has never entered.
stops.campa: The day after the constituent election, the United States Treasury designates him personally under Executive Order 13692, freezing any property under American jurisdiction and forbidding Americans to deal with him at all. It is the first American measure aimed at the man rather than at the officials around him. Whatever ordinary retirement a negotiated exit might once have offered is quietly removed by it. Nothing inside Venezuela changes on the day the designation is announced.
suggested_refs: Executive Order 13692 and the OFAC designation of 31 July 2017
sources: U.S. Department of the Treasury designation announcement, July 2017

stops.name: Palacio Federal Legislativo, Caracas: the second Constituent Assembly
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the installation (Reuters; contemporary coverage); the election itself was held 30 July 2017. Day defaults to 01. The halting of the 2016 recall referendum by procedural and judicial action, referred to in the campa, is attested by contemporary Reuters and AP reporting.
stops.campa: A recall referendum against him has already been stopped, in 2016, by procedural and judicial means before any national vote could be held, and the Tribunal has stripped the elected Assembly of its powers. Now he convenes a National Constituent Assembly with authority over everything, and the opposition boycotts the election for it. Smartmatic, the company supplying the voting machines, states afterwards that the announced turnout was inflated by at least a million votes. The new assembly takes its seats in the same building as the one it supersedes.
suggested_refs: The 2017 National Constituent Assembly and the Smartmatic statement on turnout
sources: Reuters, 'Venezuelan election turnout figures manipulated by one million votes: election company', August 2017
Contemporary Reuters and AP coverage of the 2016 recall effort

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the election of the twentieth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested (CNE announced results as reported by multiple outlets; OAS General Assembly declaration of 5 June 2018). Turnout of roughly 46 percent is as reported contemporaneously and is disputed by the opposition.
stops.campa: The presidential election is moved forward on the calendar, the strongest opposition candidates are barred from standing, and the main coalition boycotts what is left. The council announces 6,248,864 votes for Maduro, about 67.8 percent, against 1,927,958 for Henri Falcón, on a turnout near 46 percent, the lowest of the Chavista era. The opposition disputes that turnout figure too. He has been re-elected, and outside his own government almost nobody behaves as though he has. Two weeks later the General Assembly of the Organization of American States declares the process without legitimacy.
suggested_refs: The OAS General Assembly declaration of 5 June 2018 on the Venezuelan election
sources: CNE announced results as reported by multiple outlets
OAS General Assembly declaration, 5 June 2018

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the second oath
stops.date_confidence: attested (international press coverage of the January 2019 inauguration). The oath was administered before the Supreme Tribunal rather than the National Assembly, which had declared the 2018 election invalid.
stops.campa: He takes the oath for a second six-year term, not before the National Assembly, which does not recognize the election that produced it, but before the Supreme Tribunal, which does. Governments across the hemisphere recall ambassadors that week and the press corps in the hall counts which delegations came and which did not. The ceremony is correct and complete in its own terms, and the sash goes over the shoulder of a man half the hemisphere has stopped addressing as president. The term begins on the tenth of January 2019.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Tribunal of Justice of Venezuela, which administered the 2019 oath
sources: International press coverage of the January 2019 inauguration

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the balcony, twenty-third of January
stops.date_confidence: attested (widespread international coverage of the 2019 Venezuelan presidential crisis; the quotation is from Radio Universidad de Chile, 'Nicolás Maduro: ¡Aquí no se rinde nadie!', 23 January 2019).
stops.campa: Juan Guaidó, the young president of the National Assembly, stands in a square in eastern Caracas and swears himself in as interim president; Washington recognizes him within the hour and dozens of governments follow through the week. Maduro comes out onto the balcony at Miraflores, to the crowd already assembled below it, and answers that here nobody surrenders. He keeps the army, the ministries, the oil company, the courts and the territory. Guaidó keeps the recognition.
stops.quote: Decir con mucha fuerza desde Venezuela: aquí no se rinde nadie, aquí no se raja a nadie, aquí vamos a la carga, aquí vamos al combate de la paz, de la vida, de la democracia, a la victoria del futuro.
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, address from the Miraflores balcony, quoted in Radio Universidad de Chile, 23 January 2019
suggested_refs: The Miraflores balcony, from which the answer to Guaidó was given
sources: Radio Universidad de Chile, 23 January 2019
Widespread international press coverage of the 2019 crisis

stops.name: Havana: the closing speech against neoliberalism
stops.date_confidence: attested for the speech and its publication (Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Cultura, Rebelión popular contra el neoliberalismo en América Latina, 2019); tagged as reconstruction in the research pool because the venue within Havana is not specified and the pin is approximate to the city centre. The economic background in the campa is general context, not drawn from the verified pool.
stops.campa: He closes the Antiimperialist Encounter of Solidarity for Democracy and against Neoliberalism in Havana, reading the protest waves then running through Chile, Ecuador and Bolivia as the continent turning back toward the project he represents. His culture ministry prints the speech as a pamphlet. He speaks as the senior figure of a movement whose own country is years deep in economic collapse, its currency past hyperinflation, its people leaving in millions. Which hall in Havana he stood in is not recorded in any source reviewed.
suggested_refs: Rebelión popular contra el neoliberalismo en América Latina (Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Cultura, 2019), ISBN 978-980-14-4639-2
sources: Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Cultura pamphlet, 2019

stops.name: Caracas: thanking God for the dollar
stops.date_confidence: attested (MercoPress, 'Maduro publicly thanks God for the all mighty dollar as an escape valve for Venezuela's economy', 19 November 2019). The phrase 'escape valve' is the outlet's framing and not Maduro's; only the quoted portion is his.
stops.campa: Asked about the dollars that have quietly replaced the bolívar in shops, garages, rents and wages across the country, he declines to condemn them. A government that spent twenty years treating the dollar as the instrument of the enemy now treats it as the thing keeping the lights on, and the exchange controls are gone in practice long before they go on paper. He does not see it as a bad thing, he says. It can help the recovery of the country and the spread of productive forces. Thank God it exists.
stops.quote: I don't see it as a bad thing ... this process that they call 'dollarization.' It can help the recovery of the country, the spread of productive forces in the country, and the economy ... Thank God it exists.
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, remarks quoted in MercoPress, 19 November 2019
suggested_refs: The de facto dollarization of the Venezuelan economy from 2019
sources: MercoPress, 19 November 2019

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the indictment read out in Washington
stops.date_confidence: attested (U.S. Department of Justice announcement, 26 March 2020). The announcement was made in Washington; the stop sits at Maduro's own seat, where he received the news. The Barr fragment is the only wording that could be verified: justice.gov returned 403 to every automated fetch attempted, and the fuller sentence circulating in the research pool is corrupt and is not reproduced.
stops.campa: In Washington the Department of Justice unseals an indictment charging him with narco-terrorism conspiracy and with conspiring to import cocaine into the United States, alleging that he ran a structure called the Cartel de los Soles in partnership with the FARC. The Attorney General describes Venezuela under his rule as a country plagued by criminality and corruption. A reward of fifteen million dollars is posted for information leading to his arrest, and the indictment will sit open for six years. Maduro dismisses the charge from Caracas and goes on governing.
suggested_refs: The sealed 2020 SDNY indictment of Maduro and fourteen current and former Venezuelan officials
sources: U.S. Department of Justice press announcement, March 2020
Wikipedia, 'Prosecution of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores', citing the DOJ release for the Barr fragment

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the prosecutor comes to him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the announcement, contested for the day: contemporary wire reports give 3 November 2021 and en.wikipedia gives 4 November. The place is corrected: Karim Khan made the announcement in Caracas, at a joint press conference with Maduro, not at The Hague as an earlier draft of the research pool stated.
stops.campa: Karim Khan, prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, comes to Caracas, stands beside Maduro at a joint press conference, signs a memorandum of understanding with him, and announces in the same appearance that he is opening a formal investigation into crimes against humanity in Venezuela dating from at least 2017. The signing and the announcement are one event, in one room, on one afternoon. Both governments release the photograph of the two men holding the document between them.
suggested_refs: The memorandum of understanding signed in Caracas, November 2021, opening the Venezuela I investigation

stops.name: Caracas: Súper Bigote
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (The Conversation, 2021; CNN, November 2025; NBC News). Day defaults to 01. The burning of Súper Bigote effigies at the Quema de Judas is attested for Holy Week 2023 (Banca y Negocios) and is tagged as reconstruction in the research pool.
stops.campa: State television launches an animated series in which the president is a superhero whose power lives in his moustache: Súper Bigote, indestructible, beating imperialist villains in a Caracas of bright colours. By Holy Week 2023 the effigies burned at the Quema de Judas are the cartoon, burned by supporters and opponents both. The character is on murals, on caps, on T-shirts, on carnival costumes. Maduro tells his followers to use the Instagram filter of it.

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the Barbados agreement signed in his name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Congressional Research Service brief on Venezuela's 2024 election; Carter Center reporting). Day defaults to 01. The signing took place in Bridgetown, Barbados, between delegations; Maduro did not travel, so the stop sits at his own seat and the campa carries the place.
stops.campa: Delegations of his government and of the opposition sign an agreement in Bridgetown, Barbados, setting out electoral guarantees for the presidential election of 2024: international observation, a published timetable, a vote both sides can read afterwards. Maduro does not travel to Bridgetown. The signature is made in his name and the concession is his to give, and it is the last time the question of who governs Venezuela is scheduled to be answered by counting. Washington eases oil sanctions in exchange.
suggested_refs: The Barbados agreement of October 2023 on electoral guarantees
sources: Congressional Research Service brief on Venezuela's 2024 election
Carter Center reporting

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the night the tally sheets were not published
stops.date_confidence: attested for the election, the announced figures and the Carter Center finding. The location of the declaration itself, CNE headquarters or the palace, is not pinned down in the sources; Miraflores is used as his own seat on results night and the reconstruction is flagged here rather than in the prose.
stops.campa: The polls close and the council does not publish the tally sheets. Near midnight its president, Elvis Amoroso, announces at about eighty percent of transmissions that Maduro has 5,150,092 votes to Edmundo González Urrutia's 4,445,978. The station-level results never appear at all. The opposition collects printed machine actas from roughly four fifths of the polling places and puts them on the internet, where they show González at about sixty-seven percent. The Carter Center, invited to observe, reports that it cannot verify the declared result.
suggested_refs: The opposition archive of machine-printed actas from the 28 July 2024 election
sources: The Carter Center, 'Center Finds Democracy Thwarted in Venezuela' and official statement, July-August 2024

stops.name: Miraflores, Caracas: the third oath
stops.date_confidence: attested (international press coverage of the January 2025 inauguration). The Supreme Tribunal certification is dated August 2024 and the OAS General Secretariat rejection 23 August 2024. The raising of the U.S. reward to fifty million dollars is dated 7 August 2025 by the State Department announcement.
stops.campa: The Supreme Tribunal has certified the result the council never disaggregated, and the General Secretariat of the Organization of American States has rejected that certification for exactly that reason. He takes the oath anyway, a third six-year term, before the delegations still willing to attend. The mandate is unrecognized across much of the hemisphere and complete in every practical sense: the army, the ministries, the oil company, the courts. In August the United States raises the reward for information leading to his arrest to fifty million dollars.
suggested_refs: The State Department wanted poster naming Maduro head of the Cartel de los Soles
sources: International press coverage of the January 2025 inauguration

stops.name: Fuerte Tiuna, Caracas: the capture
stops.date_confidence: attested (USNI News; CBS News, 'Photos show damage at Fuerte Tiuna, the military base where Maduro was captured'; NPR, CNN live coverage). The legality of the operation under international law is disputed, including by the UN Secretary-General; that dispute is separate from the physical fact of the capture, which is not contested.
stops.campa: Helicopters of the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment come in over Fuerte Tiuna before dawn, taking fire, and put troops down inside the base where the president lives. Maduro and Cilia Flores are taken from the residence and out of the country in the same night. Delcy Rodríguez, the vice president, becomes acting president of Venezuela. The legality of the operation is disputed at once, including by the Secretary-General of the United Nations; the fact of it is not. Photographs of the damaged buildings at Fuerte Tiuna are published within the week.
suggested_refs: The damaged buildings at Fuerte Tiuna photographed after 3 January 2026

stops.name: Daniel Patrick Moynihan Courthouse, Manhattan: the arraignment
stops.date_confidence: attested (ABC News, 'Maduro declares I am innocent and still president in Manhattan court appearance'; CNBC, NBC News coverage of the 5 January 2026 arraignment). Guilt is untried and unproven; the trial is set for 1 June 2027.
stops.campa: Two days later he is walked into the federal courthouse in lower Manhattan and arraigned, his wife beside him, on narco-terrorism, cocaine-importation and weapons counts drawn from the indictment of 2020. He speaks through an interpreter. He says he is innocent, that he is a decent man, that he is still the president of his country, and he pleads not guilty to all of it. Leaving the courtroom he says he is the elected president, a prisoner of war, and that he will be free.
stops.quote: I am innocent. I am not guilty. I am a decent man. I am still president of my country.
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Maduro, arraignment before Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, quoted in ABC News, 5 January 2026

stops.name: Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn: the cell in Sunset Park
stops.date_confidence: attested for the detention (CNN, 'MDC Brooklyn: What it's like inside the infamous jail', 6 January 2026; en.wikipedia). Coordinates corrected to 80 29th Street, Sunset Park. The trial date of 1 June 2027 was set on 22 July 2026 by Judge Alvin Hellerstein in the Southern District of New York; the Eastern District attribution circulating in the research pool is an error.
stops.campa: He is held at the Metropolitan Detention Center on 29th Street in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, a federal jail with a long public record of lockdowns, violence and squalor, across one harbour from the rostrum he spoke from in 2014. Cilia Flores is held in the same complex. In July a federal judge sets the trial for the first of June, 2027. He is sixty-three years old, has been convicted of nothing, and by the spring has been inside the building for more than eighty days.
suggested_refs: The Metropolitan Detention Center, 80 29th Street, Sunset Park, Brooklyn
